tagline: Between Durango and Chama, a border drive follows narrow-gauge railroad history
intro: Tracks Across Borders runs between Durango and Chama along the Colorado–New Mexico border, crossing Southern Ute Indian Tribe reservation land and skirting Navajo Lake’s northern end. Colorado DOT gives the full drive as 125 miles and four and a half hours. In its scenic-byways program, the agency identifies the Denver and Rio Grande narrow-gauge railroad as the route’s principal story. The route includes a round-trip spur to Chimney Rock National Monument.

The railroad’s San Juan Extension was built to reach the mineral resources near Silverton. Three-foot track cost less to build and accommodated tighter curves than standard gauge. Crews reached Chama on December 31, 1880, then continued toward Durango. The Durango–Chama tracks were later removed, while the Durango–Silverton branch survived. Colorado and New Mexico bought the Chama–Antonito line, and the Cumbres and Toltec Scenic Railroad formed by 1971. Those states have jointly owned the surviving line since 1970.

From Durango, the journey reaches Ignacio, home to the Tribe’s headquarters and cultural center and museum. At Arboles, the Piedra River enters Navajo Reservoir near the state line. The road journey ends at Chama, western terminus of the Cumbres and Toltec Scenic Railroad, whose preserved line continues toward Antonito.

moments.title: Ignacio
moments.text: Ignacio is home to the Southern Ute Indian Tribe’s headquarters and the Southern Ute Cultural Center and Museum. Its Ute name is Piinuu. The town lies within a history of shrinking reservation boundaries: the Brunot Treaty removed the San Juan Mountains from the Consolidated Ute Reservation in 1873. In 1878, that reservation was replaced by the much smaller Southern Ute Indian Reservation. Ignacio’s post office opened in 1882; incorporation followed in 1913.

moments.title: Arboles
moments.text: The Piedra River’s meeting with the San Juan lies beneath Navajo Reservoir. The Piedra enters the reservoir near Arboles, whose name means trees in Spanish. Navajo Dam was completed in 1962. The rising water displaced families from Los Arboles, Los Pinos, Rose and Los Martinez. The reservoir stores and releases San Juan River water for local irrigation and the Colorado River downstream. Its Colorado shoreline is part of Navajo State Park. The park uplands have flat-topped mesas and rolling hills cut in places by steep-sided canyons. Pinyon-juniper woodland occupies dry slopes, hills and mesa tops.

moments.title: Chimney Rock National Monument
moments.text: A sandstone ridge leads toward Chimney Rock, with Companion Rock beside it. The Great House Pueblo has 36 rooms and two kivas, or round ceremonial rooms. Evidence suggests construction began in 1076 during a lunar standstill and expansion followed during another in 1093. Building materials were carried by hand up the ridge from below. The archaeological site became a national monument in 2012. The trail to the Great House begins beside a complex of three pit houses and workrooms. Excavated workrooms contained separate areas with stones for grinding corn. Peregrine falcons nest each year on Companion Rock.
